title: Things Glorious and Things Ruinous: Considering Classical Education Amidst Cultural Decay
author: Gregory Soderberg
summary: Gregory Soderberg, a veteran teacher with 20+ years in the classroom, reviews Mark Anthony Signorelli's book 'Things Glorious and Things Ruinous: Considering Classical Education Amidst Cultural Decay,' published by CiRCE Institute. The review argues the book is essential summer reading for any teacher and articulates the core tension between modern education's economic and utilitarian aims and classical education's goal of bringing students into right relationship with truth, goodness, and beauty. Signorelli, drawing on the liberal arts tradition, argues that the modern emphasis on demonstrating measurable outcomes misunderstands what education is fundamentally for — not producing or demonstrating, but receiving. The review highlights Signorelli's argument that classical education is uniquely inclusive because its measure is receptivity rather than performance, allowing students of very different aptitudes to benefit from the same program. The piece also engages Signorelli's treatment of child development, writing instruction, and the proper place of classical schooling in a culturally decaying society.
points: The book's central argument pits modern education's purpose — preparing students for the workplace and competitive marketplace — against classical education's purpose: bringing children into right encounter with being for the kinds of beings they are.

Signorelli argues that classical education's metric of receptivity rather than performance output makes it uniquely inclusive across ability levels. When what matters is what students can take away rather than what they bring, a wide range of aptitudes can flourish in the same classroom.

The modern system's 'unhealthy obsession with testing metrics constantly requires young people to demonstrate what they can give.' Classical education asks only that students show up ready to receive — a fundamentally different relationship between student and knowledge.

Teaching children about historical injustice without the goal of building awareness of their own capacity for wrongdoing is, in Signorelli's view, a pedagogical failure: the purpose of studying evil is to cultivate resistance to it in oneself, not to sort students into victim and perpetrator categories.

The book's structure — Theoria, the Liberal Arts Tradition, Child Development, Classical Education in Society, Pedagogy, and Writing Instruction — makes it a comprehensive practitioner resource as well as a philosophical argument for the classical vision.
quotes: This is a beautiful book. The design and paper type show clear concern for excellence from CiRCE, the publisher. It's also beautifully written. Signorelli has a background in literature and it shows.
'Modern education prepares students for the workplace. Classical education prepares them for life.'

'The classical educator only claims to offer her students the right kind of encounter with being for the kind of beings they are. She only says that her program of study brings children into regular contact with truth, goodness, and beauty because children desire, above all things, truth, goodness, and beauty.'

'The modern education system, with its stupid and unhealthy obsession with testing metrics, constantly requires young people to demonstrate what they can give. But the classical school only asks the student to show up ready to receive.'

'If the significant thing is not what students bring to their studies but what they can take away, then a considerable disparity in talents can be accommodated in classrooms where engagement is prioritized above all things.'

'The only possible justification for teaching young minds about the horrid injustice that men have inflicted upon one another is to awaken them to an awareness of their own potential to carry out such injustices and to begin to cultivate in their souls some resistance to that propensity.'
